title: Mamdani Condemns Racism Against Indian Americans at New York Diwali Event
excerpt: Hosting Diwali at his office, New York's first Indian-American mayor cited attacks on Hindu temples and Sikh Americans and urged a rejection of a “politics of darkness.”
body:
• New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani condemned rising racism against Indian Americans at a Diwali celebration hosted by his office on Tuesday, saying, “We have the responsibility to banish that hatred.”
  • He cited a year of incidents targeting Hindu temples and Sikh Americans, and hate moving from the margins into mainstream political campaigns.
  • The same day, 13 US lawmakers asked federal agencies to examine whether the November 7 disruption of a Seattle Diwali celebration was a federal hate crime, and sought a briefing by December 4.
  • A study cited in the lawmakers' letter counted more than 542,000 anti-South Asian hateful posts on X between January 2025 and June 2026; one in four Indian Americans reported being called a slur since 2025.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani denounced the surge in racism against the Indian-American community during a Diwali celebration hosted by his office on Tuesday, asserting that “we have the responsibility to banish that hatred,” ANI reported.

Addressing the gathering, Mamdani drew attention to multiple incidents directed at Hindus and Sikhs over the last 12 months. “This past year alone, we have seen our Hindu temple targeted. We have seen leaders at the highest levels of our federal government target Sikhs. And we have watched as hate that was once relegated to the margins of society has come to sit at the heart of campaigns for statewide office,” he said, urging a repudiation of what he called a “politics of darkness.”

"We have the responsibility to banish that hatred. We all have the responsibility to ensure that Hindu-Americans can live here in safety and in peace and can worship their religion as is their right."

— Zohran Mamdani, Mayor of New York City

Mamdani had made a similar appeal at a Durga Puja celebration, where he referred to an attempted mass shooting at a Hindu temple in Illinois and said Hindu Americans must be able to worship and participate in religious activities safely, The India Print reported.

A personal connection to the festival

Mamdani, the first Indian-American mayor of the country's most populous city, spoke about his own connection to Diwali. “It is truly the honour and privilege of a lifetime to host all of you here and to be here as the first Indian American Mayor in the history of our city. As someone who grew up celebrating Diwali with my family, to now be able to celebrate it with our city as mayor is a gift I will never grow tired of saying thank you for,” he said. His mother, the filmmaker Mira Nair, hails from a Punjabi Hindu background. The 35-year-old also spoke of his respect for the Ramayana and the Mahabharata: “The Ramayana shows us the brother, wife, husband and friend we desire to be. The Mahabharata shows us what families are really like, where even the bravest heroes and wisest gods stumble and where one's dharma must come before one's loyalty.”

Lawmakers press Washington over the Seattle disruption

Mamdani's remarks coincided with a letter made public on Tuesday in which 13 members of the US House of Representatives — including all six Indian-American lawmakers — asked law enforcement officials to examine whether the disruption of a Seattle Diwali event by two far-right influencers constituted a federal hate crime. We covered the letter in detail in our report on the federal probe sought into the Seattle Diwali disruption. The letter, led by Representatives Pramila Jayapal, Raja Krishnamoorthi and Grace Meng, was addressed to Attorney General Todd Blanche with a copy to FBI Director Kash Patel, and it asked the administration for a briefing by December 4 on the investigation and on measures to prevent further attacks. The lawmakers' request is for an investigation; the Seattle incident has not been established as a federal hate crime.

The scale of online hate

The letter cited a September 2026 study by the Centre for the Study of Organised Hate, which identified more than 542,000 anti-South Asian hateful posts on X between January 2025 and June 2026. “One in four Indian Americans report being called a slur since 2025, and nearly one in five have avoided wearing Indian dress in public,” the lawmakers wrote.

What happens next

The next marker is the administration's response to the lawmakers: whether the Justice Department opens an examination of the Seattle incident, and what the requested December 4 briefing produces on federal measures against anti-South Asian hate. For community organisations, Mamdani's remarks add the mayor of the country's largest city to the public officials now on record calling temple and festival security a shared civic responsibility.
